doc.title: Chico Hamilton — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

chapter: Day two: LA youth and army revisited
title: Hospitalized in the psychiatric ward after seeing so many black soldiers
summary: Culture shock from seeing so many black people landed him in the psychiatric ward for two or three weeks.

story.theme_name: Drafted: musicians in the military and the war years
story.community_name: Drafted: service bands, USO shows and the war years

blocks.x: That was the truth and it probably could still be considered the truth. Now you said that when you got in the army, you got to Fort McClellan in Alabama, you said that was the first thing you saw, a great mass of black people.
And you said you had to go through, what was it; you got some sort of treatment?
Oh, man I had to go to the psycho ward.

Really. It affected me. And that probably sounds strange coming from, you know, a black dude but it was just -- that’s the affect. I’m being honest about it, you know. As a matter of fact I can talk about it.

I mean I’m saying, you know, I’m cool now about it but it was unbelievable man. And I found out, you know, a lot of things about being a black man and I found out man, that we had a lot of brilliant people man, a lot of brilliant people were black.

So the psycho ward -- I mean obviously if you’re in the military and as a vet I guess I could probably speak with experience, if you’re sent to the psycho ward you’re going to probably speak to either a social worker, or a psychologist, or a psychiatrist.
And back in those days, you know, I want to say -­
White psychologist, and you’re going to tell them; I have problems being around so many black people. Was it helpful?
Well I stayed in the hospital for about two or three weeks.
